examples.heading: Command examples

examples.heading: overview
examples.description: Select the agent whose configuration you want to understand. This is the application overview, useful before deciding whether a missing response is caused by configuration or by current work. It requires no ready model.

examples.heading: diagnostics.get
examples.description: Use this after recording the failed conversation or work ID. You must own the agent, and the private runtime must be reachable; the command can start a suspended worker, so it is unsuitable for passive dormancy monitoring.

examples.heading: usage.summary
examples.description: Run this after actual work, or while investigating a timeout. Keep the work ID available so you can compare its direct consumption with held allocations. A provider subscription or billing connection is not required.

examples.heading: conversations.create
examples.description: Create a new thread inside the already selected agent. A model need not be ready merely to create the conversation. Use a meaningful title; creating another conversation does not create another agent or private workspace.

examples.heading: conversations.list
examples.description: Choose a search term that occurs in the intended conversation title or recorded user-message text. Assistant-output text is not searched by this command. Set include_archived true when you want a thread removed from the active sidebar.

examples.heading: conversations.get
examples.description: Take the conversation ID from conversations.list or a successful creation response. Use this to inspect one thread before renaming it, checking accepted messages, or connecting a workflow to its history.

examples.heading: conversations.update
examples.description: Read the current conversation and revision first. This example renames an existing thread. Use the same command with archived true to archive it or archived false to restore a conversation to the active list.

examples.heading: messages.send
examples.description: Use an existing active conversation. For this source-summary example, first upload and attach the intended source, or include actual attachment IDs in the optional attachments array. Choose a fresh message ID for this exact input.

examples.heading: messages.cancel
examples.description: Identify the conversation whose active work you want stopped. The message_id here identifies the cancellation request itself; it is not the ID of the earlier prompt. Keep it stable if that cancellation acknowledgement is lost.

examples.heading: messages.events
examples.description: Use a conversation ID to limit replay, or omit it for the agent's public conversation stream. Start after zero for available history, then retain the returned cursor for subsequent pages instead of repeatedly processing old events.

examples.heading: attachments.upload
examples.description: Prepare a plain filename, canonical media type, and bytes within the 4 MiB upload bound. The supplied base64 is Hello followed by a newline. Choose one operation ID for these exact original bytes and metadata.

examples.heading: attachments.list
examples.description: Use this to find source IDs after an upload or when rebuilding a conversation's attachment selection. The example requests twenty records; the command does not search arbitrary host directories or other agents' libraries.

examples.heading: attachments.get
examples.description: Copy an attachment ID from upload or list. This command is appropriate when you need the original artifact reference, media type, size, or extraction status before deciding whether to index or transcribe the source.

examples.heading: attachments.read
examples.description: Obtain the attachment ID from metadata and choose a nonnegative byte offset. The example reads at most 4,096 original bytes, useful for checking a source prefix without claiming that the entire file was included.

examples.heading: artifacts.read
examples.description: Take a real artifact ID from attachment metadata or a tool result, such as generated audio or a screenshot. Use this recipe for immutable bytes; it does not edit the artifact or require a workspace file with that name.

examples.heading: files.list
examples.description: Choose a workspace-relative directory. The example lists the public workspace root. Internal .sturgis entries and path escapes are excluded; this interface does not expose the installation root, vault directory, or another agent's files.

examples.heading: files.read
examples.description: Choose a regular public workspace file found through files.list. Read it before editing or deleting so that the subsequent mutation can protect the exact bytes you reviewed, even if another writer is active.

examples.heading: files.write
examples.description: Use a new public workspace path for this create example. The base64 writes Hello and a newline. To replace an existing file, first read it and add its current exact hash as expected_sha256.

examples.heading: files.delete
examples.description: Read the file and preserve any copy you need before deleting. Replace CURRENT_SHA256 with the exact returned 64-character SHA-256, not the hash of an older version or the string shown in this example.

examples.heading: knowledge.add
examples.description: Upload a supported source and confirm extraction is ready. The example creates a new knowledge document from that attachment. For a new revision of an existing document, also provide document_id and its current expected_revision.

examples.heading: knowledge.list
examples.description: Choose a term appearing in document titles or extracted text. This lists current nondeleted knowledge documents; it does not search all conversation history or enumerate the immutable source library underneath those documents.

examples.heading: knowledge.get
examples.description: Use a document ID from knowledge.list. The example explicitly requests revision one to inspect historical source text. Omit revision when you need the latest record and concurrency revision for a new edit or deletion.

examples.heading: knowledge.delete
examples.description: Inspect the current document and confirm that removing its knowledge index is intended. Supply the current expected_revision and a stable operation ID. This is not an attachment-delete command or a way to erase all historical evidence.

examples.heading: memory.query
examples.description: Choose a term or concept you want to recall. A model provider need not be ready, but the native memory process must be available. The example uses lexical text only; embeddings require a compatible model and vector dimension.

examples.heading: memory.get
examples.description: Copy an actual memory ID from query results. The example requests canonical revision one, which is useful when understanding a correction. Omit revision to retrieve the latest canonical version rather than relying on an old search result.

examples.heading: memory.correct
examples.description: Verify the original evidence, then retrieve the current unretracted canonical record. Supply its revision and the complete intended correction. The example changes a date; it does not claim the server independently checked the corrected external source.

examples.heading: memory.retract
examples.description: Inspect the memory and decide whether you mean one revision or its entire identity. The example explicitly withdraws revision two. Removing revision from the parameters suppresses all revisions of this identity, including future revisions.

examples.heading: goals.create
examples.description: State a desired outcome and choose explicit nonnegative resource limits. The example reserves no execution by itself; it creates the intention that later scheduled or planned work can reference through goal_id.

examples.heading: goals.list
examples.description: Use this before editing, activating, pausing, or archiving goals. It reads goal records for the selected agent and is independent of whether a provider can currently run the next model turn.

examples.heading: goals.edit
examples.description: Retrieve a nonterminal goal and its current revision. The example changes only the objective. To change limits or criteria, supply those fields explicitly after reviewing existing usage, outstanding reservations, and what the revised outcome is meant to establish.

examples.heading: goals.transition
examples.description: Use the shown active transition only for a proposed or otherwise resumable goal, with its current revision. Activation permits eligible associated resource reservations; it does not automatically create a plan, schedule, or model conversation.

examples.heading: goals.archive
examples.description: Use a goal already in achieved, failed, or abandoned state. Read its current revision and verify you intend to remove it from normal active goal management. Archiving a live goal is rejected.

examples.heading: commitments.create
examples.description: Describe the responsibility and intended beneficiary. The example uses owner, which is also the consumer default. Optional criteria should specify real fulfillment checks; an optional expiry is a time for assessing overdue responsibility, not automatic execution.

examples.heading: commitments.list
examples.description: Use this when reviewing accepted responsibilities, checking blocked progress, or finding the current revision and wait identity. It reads commitment state without requiring you to infer responsibility from conversation wording.

examples.heading: commitments.transition
examples.description: Read the proposal and use its current revision for the shown accepted transition. The state change makes an explicit responsibility; it still does not supply compute, schedule a task, or prove any result.

examples.heading: commitments.progress
examples.description: Use an accepted commitment without an active durable wait. The example marks it blocked with a concrete reason. Supported manual progress values are pending, in_progress, and blocked; waiting is established through commitments.wait.

examples.heading: commitments.wait
examples.description: Use an accepted responsibility with no existing wait. Select an actual conversation for the user_response trigger. Replace after_seq zero with the observed current cursor if you intend to wait only for a future response.

examples.heading: commitments.resume
examples.description: Retrieve the accepted waiting commitment and its current revision after the registered trigger has actually fired. This is the follow-up to a matching durable wait, not a general way to restart any blocked responsibility.

examples.heading: schedules.create
examples.description: Choose an existing active conversation, actual prompt, and positive model-work allocation. The example schedules weekday mornings in Europe/Berlin, with Monday zero through Friday four, and an explicit first-occurrence daylight-saving fold policy.

examples.heading: schedules.list
examples.description: Use this before changing a timer or checking whether future work can wake a suspended agent. Keep the conversation and goal relationship in view so you know where each occurrence will be admitted.

examples.heading: schedules.state
examples.description: Read the schedule's current revision. The example pauses a live schedule; use active to resume an eligible paused one or cancelled to terminate it. Neither state nor revision should be guessed from an old screenshot.

examples.heading: workflows.create
examples.description: Define the step descriptions, dependency graph, and shared budget before creating a plan. This one-step example has its own allocation matching the shared allowance. Omitted assignee defaults to the agent; creation alone does not start execution.

examples.heading: workflows.list
examples.description: Use this to discover saved plans before choosing one to run, pause, revise, or inspect. The list belongs to the selected agent; a goal or commitment is not itself a workflow record.

examples.heading: workflows.get
examples.description: Take a real plan ID from creation or listing. Inspect it before recovering a failed step, because the plan state, individual step state, and recorded execution run can describe different parts of the same interruption.

examples.heading: workflows.revise
examples.description: Read a live plan with no in-progress steps and supply the complete desired step list plus a reason. The example applies only to a one-step plan; including it verbatim in a larger plan would replace that larger definition.

examples.heading: workflows.run
examples.description: Choose an active plan and an existing nonarchived conversation. Supply the plan's current revision. Check provider readiness, associated goal state, resources, and required permissions before asking the monitor to admit ready steps.

examples.heading: workflows.state
examples.description: Retrieve the current plan revision. Use the shown paused transition for an active plan. Active resumes a paused plan; abandoned requires a reason and ends a live intention. These are plan lifecycle states, separate from step progress.

examples.heading: workflows.step
examples.description: This recipe requires an active plan with a pending human_review step explicitly assigned as {"kind":"user"} and completed dependencies. Create that definition with workflows.create or revise a suitable live plan before using its ID here.

examples.heading: work.overview
examples.description: Use this when you need one view of the agent's work domains rather than provider settings. It can help connect a pending task to its goal, commitment, timer, workflow, child, or initiative proposal.

examples.heading: work.list
examples.description: Run this after a prompt or timer has been admitted and you need its scheduler work ID. The provider may still be unavailable; queued execution can remain recorded while its admission requirements are unresolved.

examples.heading: work.get
examples.description: Use the scheduler work ID found in list, message admission, or workflow evidence. A goal, conversation, or tool attempt ID is a different identity and cannot be substituted for this lookup.

examples.heading: work.cancel
examples.description: Identify the exact nonterminal work you intend to end and provide a useful reason. Use message cancellation when your intention is conversation-wide; this command operates from a specific scheduler work record and its affected lineage.

examples.heading: children.delegate
examples.description: Use an actual eligible live parent work record with sufficient remaining resources and delegable capabilities. This example grants no tool capabilities; include the bounded material needed for review in the supported task description rather than assuming parent files are inherited.

examples.heading: children.list
examples.description: Use this after delegated work exists, or when checking whether a parent cancellation affected its children. The web Inbox also exposes delegated records, but this command provides their actual IDs for precise inspection.

examples.heading: children.get
examples.description: Copy a child record ID from children.list. Use it to inspect the delegation itself; use the returned work_id with work.get when investigating scheduler execution or resource consumption underneath that child.

examples.heading: children.cancel
examples.description: Identify the child you no longer need, review any active external attempt, and choose a reason that explains the parent's decision. This is a child cancellation request, not deletion of a top-level user agent.

examples.heading: initiative.propose
examples.description: Choose an actual source event from this agent and a concrete proposed action. Supply all six finite signals between zero and one, a future expiry, and a stable dedupe key for that particular source/action opportunity.

examples.heading: attention.policy
examples.description: Choose the desired proactive policy and read the last saved policy revision. The example uses suggest with a score threshold and expected revision zero only for an absent policy. It does not enable autonomous execution.

examples.heading: inbox.list
examples.description: Use this after the monitor has evaluated initiative candidates or when the web Inbox shows a proposal. No ready provider is needed simply to inspect what was proposed and why attention selected a particular disposition.

examples.heading: inbox.decide
examples.description: Inspect a pending proposal before deciding. The example dismisses it and requires no execution resources. To accept, use decision accept with an active conversation_id and an explicit positive resources allocation suitable for the proposed prompt.

examples.heading: providers.configure
examples.description: Obtain the exact streaming chat-completions endpoint, model name, and documented limits from the service operator. The example deliberately configures text-only behavior; it names no bundled model.

examples.heading: providers.list
examples.description: Use this to discover saved provider IDs and determine which configuration is selected. It reads configuration and recorded probe evidence rather than issuing a fresh inference request.

examples.heading: providers.inspect
examples.description: Take a provider_id from the list. The example inspects research only; omitting provider_id returns all configurations, matching providers.list. Use this before editing or activating a particular revision.

examples.heading: providers.probe
examples.description: Read the current configuration revision and confirm its credential is still current. This performs a real bounded inference request and can consume provider resources, even though it does not execute a model-proposed tool.

examples.heading: providers.activate
examples.description: Choose a provider with a successful unexpired probe for its current configuration and credential revision. Use that configuration revision, not the separate probe record's revision, in this request.

examples.heading: providers.credentials.put
examples.description: Use the dedicated credential command so the secret is requested privately and never placed in a parameters file or shell argument. The example creates model_key; rotation adds --revision with the current credential revision.

examples.heading: providers.credentials.list
examples.description: Use this to choose a stored opaque credential reference or obtain the current revision before rotation or revocation. It requires owner access to this agent, not a model task.

examples.heading: providers.credentials.revoke
examples.description: Inspect the credential's current revision and identify dependent providers or connections before revocation. Use this when the old value should no longer authorize future requests from the agent.

examples.heading: connections.configure
examples.description: Choose a supported adapter kind and a real compatible endpoint. This example defines HTTP fetch; optional allowed_origins defaults to the endpoint's exact origin, while credentials use opaque current vault references.

examples.heading: connections.list
examples.description: Use this to discover configured connection IDs and readiness states. It reads local records; it does not fetch every endpoint or automatically grant operations simply because the owner saved an address.

examples.heading: connections.get
examples.description: Use a connection ID from configuration or list. Inspect it before editing, granting, probing, signing external traffic, or revoking; each of those operations depends on the exact current binding.

examples.heading: connections.grant
examples.description: Read the connection revision and select only operations offered by its adapter. HTTP uses fetch; MCP uses call; webhook uses receive. This example grants the reference fetch connection its single read operation.

examples.heading: connections.probe
examples.description: Read the active connection's current revision after configuration and grants. Ensure its credential is current. The probe may contact a real service and is an observation, not a universal harmless health endpoint.

examples.heading: connections.revoke
examples.description: Inspect the selected connection and current revision before removing future access. Use this for all its operations rather than attempting to grant an empty operation list. Consider any already submitted external requests.

examples.heading: devices.list
examples.description: Use this after configuring device-kind connections, or when checking which compatible clients have paired. It does not discover arbitrary computers on the local network or install actuator software.

examples.heading: devices.get
examples.description: Use the connection_id of a device-kind connection. It differs from the external client's device_id and from a pending device request ID. Read it before pairing, signing at a revision, or revoking.

examples.heading: devices.pair
examples.description: Configure the device identity and operation schemas first, then read its connection revision. This recipe writes the full one-time pairing response to a new private file because normal CLI output redacts recognized token fields.

examples.heading: devices.revoke
examples.description: Read the device connection's current revision and verify this is the client whose future access should end. Revocation is distinct from cancelling one outstanding operation or deleting a computer's installed client software.

examples.heading: permissions.list
examples.description: Use this before changing a tool policy. The list reflects tools currently registered through built-ins, ready connections, or active plugins; it is not an unbounded catalog of every tool a model might name.

examples.heading: permissions.set
examples.description: Read the current workspace.write policy revision and descriptor. The example sets ask only when revision zero denotes no saved policy; substitute the observed policy revision for an existing setting.

examples.heading: permissions.pending
examples.description: Use this after a model action was rejected with approval_required. It projects only requests that remain pending from trusted tool-runner rejection evidence. Use permissions.request with a saved event ID to inspect a later decision or stale/expired state.

examples.heading: permissions.request
examples.description: Take an event_id from the pending request projection. It must identify the trusted rejected invocation itself, not a conversation message, proposed goal, or unrelated successful tool result.

examples.heading: permissions.approve
examples.description: Inspect the exact pending request and confirm the proposed arguments and constraints. The example gives its matching future invocation a 300-second window; the supported expiry range is one to 3,600 seconds.

examples.heading: permissions.deny
examples.description: Use the actual request event after inspecting its proposed tool, arguments, and binding. Deny this invocation when it should not receive one-use authority; changing the general tool policy is a separate decision.

examples.heading: skills.install
examples.description: Prepare a bounded manifest with id, version, description, triggers, steps, and required_tools. This example installs instructions for source review with no required tools; it is a procedure, not executable plugin code.

examples.heading: skills.list
examples.description: Use this to inspect available authored or discovered procedures before enabling, disabling, or choosing a prior version. IDs are normalized for the consumer view; private host discovery paths are omitted.

examples.heading: skills.enable
examples.description: Choose a stored procedure with an actual current revision. This example disables review_sources using enabled false; use true after review when you want that stored procedure eligible for selection again.

examples.heading: skills.rollback
examples.description: Inspect the stored procedure and verify a prior version exists. Use the current record revision; this is distinct from the human-selected manifest version string such as 1 or 2.

examples.heading: plugins.list
examples.description: Use this only to discover plugins already installed by an operator. The consumer surface does not download arbitrary packages, install from a URL, or provide a public marketplace through this command.

examples.heading: plugins.inspect
examples.description: Choose an actual installed plugin ID and inspect it before activation, rollback, or uninstall. This is the safe metadata step for an inactive package; plugins.health instead requires an active plugin.

examples.heading: plugins.activate
examples.description: Inspect an operator-installed package and use its current record revision. Activation executes its lifecycle backend and can change plugin state; trust in installed code is an operator responsibility.

examples.heading: plugins.health
examples.description: Run this only after metadata reports status active. It invokes the active plugin's health backend, so it is not a purely local inspection of an inactive installation.

examples.heading: plugins.disable
examples.description: Inspect the active plugin and use its current revision when you intend to remove future use. The host drains its active lifecycle before completing deactivation; this is more than a presentation toggle.

examples.heading: plugins.rollback
examples.description: Confirm metadata contains a compatible retained previous active version/state, then use the current plugin revision. This is a deliberate return to that retained executable state, not an arbitrary version selector.

examples.heading: plugins.uninstall
examples.description: Inspect the plugin first. It must be installed, disabled, or quarantined with no pending transition; an active plugin must be disabled and drained before uninstall. Use the current revision after that lifecycle change.
